headline: A judge stops the Trump ads taxpayers paid for
summary: A federal judge ordered the Trump administration on Sunday to stop running taxpayer-funded TV ads that feature the president. Common Cause and Democracy Forward sued; the DNC has a similar case in Washington. The White House calls the ads public service announcements. Trump has said he'll pay for them himself. A hearing is set for Oct. 13.
cover_answer: Taxpayers. A judge says that stops now.
table_question: Can you use the group's money to tell people how great you are?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: The government has been putting ads on TV with the president in them, and paying with tax money, the money everyone pays in, like coins in one big jar. On Sunday a judge said: stop, for now. Some groups say the rules don't allow it. The judge hears more on Tuesday, and the grown-ups have it.
5-7.why: One jar everyone fills. The judge is the grown-up who said stop.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old reasons from what is in front of them, so the script turns tax money into one jar everyone pays into, and the judge into the grown-up who said stop. The lawsuits and the midterms stay out. Expect "is the president in trouble?" Not yet. A judge said stop for now, and there's a meeting about it Tuesday.

8-12.script: The Trump administration ran TV ads starring the president and paid with tax money. Watchdog groups sued: Congress never allowed it, and the rules bar propaganda. On Sunday a judge said they'd probably win and stopped the ads. A referee can halt play before the final call.
8-12.why: Ads, tax money, lawsuit, order. The whistle is the mechanism.
8-12.why_long: This age is working out rules and whether adults apply them to themselves, so the script runs the chain: ads with the president in them, tax money, a lawsuit, an order. The referee's whistle is the mechanism, play stopped before the final call. Expect "did he break the law?" A judge thinks the groups will probably win. The case isn't over.

13-17.script: Where is the line between a public service announcement and a campaign ad on the taxpayer's tab? The White House says every administration advertises; the groups say these star the president before the midterms. Second: Trump promised to pay. The White House won't refund. Does that count?
13-17.why: The line, then the promise against the money gone.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once: governments have always advertised their policies, and these ads star the president before an election. The script asks where the line is, then sets Trump's promise to pay against a White House that won't refund. Expect "who decides what's propaganda?" The judge, for now. Hearing Oct. 13.

5-7.a: A judge in New York whose job is to decide whether the rules were followed. She said stop, for now. The grown-ups have it.

8-12.a: Taxpayers. Trump said he'd pay himself. The White House won't refund.

8-12.q: Why is it against the rules?
8-12.a: The groups say Congress never approved it, and the rules bar propaganda.

13-17.a: The White House says yes, both parties. The groups say these star Trump himself.
The order is temporary. A hearing is set for Oct. 13.
